findings.title: Don't pipe unpinned remote script to sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: The build now fetches https://example.com/install.sh at image-build time and pipes it directly into `sh` running as root. There is no version pin, checksum, or signature check, so whoever controls that host (or the network, since no TLS pin/verification guarantee is expressed beyond curl defaults) can execute arbitrary code inside the built image. It also makes the image non-reproducible: the same commit can build different images over time, and a compromised or changed upstream silently ships into production. Supply-chain surface (install/build script) is explicitly in scope.

findings.title: curl -sL without --fail hides download failure, feeds error body to sh
findings.whyItBreaks: curl without `-f/--fail` exits 0 on HTTP 4xx/5xx and writes the error body (e.g. a 404 HTML page) to stdout, which `sh` then executes. Additionally, in `curl ... | sh` the pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s, not curl's, so a failed/empty download is not surfaced as a build failure (absent `set -o pipefail`). Previously a plain `curl -fsSL ... && sh` would abort the RUN on a fetch failure; now the build can silently continue with nothing (or garbage) installed, producing an image missing the intended tooling and failing later at runtime.

findings.title: Piping unpinned remote install.sh into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches a mutable, unsigned, unchecksummed script over the network and executes it as root inside the image build. There is no version/commit pin, no hash verification, and no TLS pinning, so any change or compromise of the remote host (or DNS/MITM) yields arbitrary code execution and a non-reproducible image. Every rebuild can run different code with no reviewable artifact in the repo.

findings.title: curl|sh hides download failure, build proceeds silently
findings.whyItBreaks: In `curl ... | sh`, the pipeline exit status is that of `sh`, not `curl`. If the fetch fails (network error, DNS, TLS), curl writes nothing to stdout, `sh` reads EOF and exits 0, so the `RUN` succeeds and the image builds without the tool installed. Worse, `-s` suppresses curl's error output and there is no `-f`, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx body (e.g. an error page) is still piped into `sh` and can execute. The failure is indistinguishable from success at the build layer.

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into shell during build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new line `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and executes arbitrary remote content as root inside the image build with no version pin, checksum, or signature. Any compromise of the endpoint or an on-path attacker turns into code execution baked into the shipped image, and the build is non-reproducible because the fetched content can change between builds.

findings.title: Build succeeds even when install script download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL ... | sh` runs under `/bin/sh -c` with no `pipefail`, so the RUN exit status is `sh`'s, not curl's. `-s` suppresses errors and there is no `-f`, so an HTTP error (e.g. 404/500) still exits 0 and can feed an error body to `sh`; a connection failure feeds empty input to `sh`, which typically exits 0. The build therefore reports success while the intended install never happened, producing an image that is missing or partially configured with no failure signal.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault calls Load and discards its error (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`). Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent (src/store.go:8-10). The function therefore returns "" for a missing key, which is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. Because the function is exported (public contract), every caller is forced to conflate "key absent / lookup failed" with "value is empty", so a caller that persists, bills, or reports the result cannot detect the failure case. The swallow is the defect itself, independent of whether any in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines send; breaks completion contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run blocked on `results <- j*2` for every job, so when Run returned, all len(jobs) values had been handed to the channel. The new code launches a goroutine per job and returns immediately without any WaitGroup/channel-close synchronization. A caller that treats Run as synchronous (the only reasonable reading of the unchanged signature `Run(ctx, jobs, results)`) now observes two concrete failures: (1) results are not yet delivered when Run returns, so reading results afterward yields missing/zero values; (2) the common pattern `Run(...); close(results)` (or a receiver that closes on seeing expected count) closes the channel while spawned goroutines are still executing `results <- j*2`, producing `panic: send on closed channel`. Additionally, if the receiver stops reading, goroutines block forever on the unbuffered/partially-consumed send, leaking a goroutine per job with no bound and no ctx cancellation. The goroutine-per-job spawn is also unbounded (one per element of jobs), so a large jobs slice now creates unbounded concurrent senders.

findings.title: Run returns before jobs finish; results may be lost or race a close
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run blocked until every job had been delivered to results, so a caller could rely on all results being present (and on it being safe to close/consume the channel) once Run returned. The new body launches one detached goroutine per job and returns immediately, so Run no longer waits for any send. A caller that closes results after Run returns (the standard fan-out pattern) can panic with 'send on closed channel', and a caller that reads len(jobs) values after Run returns can observe zero/incomplete results. The public function name/behavior ('Run the jobs') is the contract, and the body no longer honors it; the results a caller receives are affected, so this is a defect even with no in-repo caller yet.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutine spawn and leak on blocked send
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop spawns len(jobs) goroutines with no concurrency bound, so a large jobs slice creates unbounded goroutines. Each goroutine sends to results with no ctx.Done() select; if results is unbuffered or not drained concurrently, the goroutines block forever. Because Run no longer waits, those blocked goroutines are leaked silently instead of applying backpressure, and the passed ctx is never consulted so cancellation cannot stop them.

findings.title: Run returns before results are delivered (lost results / send-on-closed panic)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior: `results <- j*2` ran inline, so when Run returned every job's result had been sent and the caller could safely close/range results. The change (src/worker.go:7-9) launches detached goroutines and returns immediately, so return no longer means completion. A caller doing `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results); for r := range results {}` will close the channel while a goroutine is still on `results <- j*2`, causing `panic: send on closed channel`; a caller that inspects results after return will silently see fewer than len(jobs) values. There is no WaitGroup or completion signal to restore the guarantee.

findings.title: Unbounded detached goroutines leak; ctx cancellation ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: Each loop iteration spawns a goroutine that blocks on `results <- j*2` (src/worker.go:7-9). If the consumer stops reading, or `results` is unbuffered and the receiver returns early, every blocked goroutine leaks permanently: ctx is never observed and there is no select/cancellation path. Previously the blocking send executed in Run's own goroutine, so the caller retained control. A large `jobs` slice also creates len(jobs) concurrent goroutines with no bound, and cancellation cannot stop any of them.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now allows non-admins and cross-tenant deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required BOTH admin AND same-tenant (session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId). With `||`, the guard returns true in two illegitimate cases: (1) a non-admin user in the same tenant as the record (session.isAdmin=false, tenantId matches) is now allowed to delete it — a privilege-escalation bypass of the admin requirement; (2) an admin in ANY tenant (session.isAdmin=true, tenantId differs) can now delete records belonging to other tenants — a cross-tenant data-destruction bypass. Substituting real values: {isAdmin:false, sessionTenant:'A', recordTenant:'A'} → true (was false, should be false); {isAdmin:true, sessionTenant:'A', recordTenant:'B'} → true (was false, should be false). The function is exported/public and is the sole authorization carrier for the delete decision, so the broken contract ships even with no in-repo caller.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR-logic lets any user delete records they must not
findings.whyItBreaks: The base predicate required `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, i.e. only an admin acting within their own tenant could delete. The head replaces `&&` with `||`, so the guard now passes if EITHER condition holds: (1) any admin can delete a record in ANY tenant (cross-tenant privilege escalation, since `session.tenantId === record.tenantId` is no longer required for admins); (2) any non-admin can delete ANY record in their own tenant regardless of `record.ownerId` (the ownerId field is never consulted), so a regular user can delete other users' records in the same tenant. The base code's conjunction is the obvious intended policy; this is an authorization bypass, not a tightening.

findings.title: Restore && in canDeleteRecord; || is an authorization bypass
findings.whyItBreaks: The base predicate was `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, i.e. only a tenant admin may delete a record in their own tenant. Changing it to `||` makes the predicate true when EITHER condition holds, so it grants two unauthorized deletes: (1) session.isAdmin=true with any tenantId returns true, allowing cross-tenant deletion by an admin (tenant isolation broken); (2) session.isAdmin=false with session.tenantId===record.tenantId returns true, allowing any non-admin user in the tenant to delete records (privilege escalation). Truth table: admin+same=true (unchanged), admin+different=true (was false), non-admin+same=true (was false), non-admin+different=false (unchanged). The exported canDeleteRecord is the authorization decision for a destructive operation, so any caller now over-authorizes.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse/validation errors, losing user settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all converts every failure (malformed JSON, bad theme, bad fontSize) into { ...DEFAULTS }. parseSettings is exported and its only live caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) cannot distinguish the fallback from valid data, then persists it at src/settings.ts:22. Before this change the throw propagated out of parseSettings (base lines 9-12) through updateFontSize (base line 16) and save() was never reached, preserving the on-disk file. Now a corrupt/partially-written file like '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"oops"}' makes updateFontSize write back {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, silently discarding the user's theme and any other stored settings — a lost write.

Now the failure is indistinguishable from valid settings: updateFontSize proceeds to `settings.fontSize = size` and `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` (src/settings.ts:21-22), persisting `{"theme":"light",...}` and permanently discarding the user's existing theme whenever the raw blob is transiently corrupt or partially written. The original error signal never reaches any caller, so no one can log, retry, or surface it.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors; updateFontSize overwrites settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new bare `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS } }` converts every malformed-input failure (invalid JSON, non-string theme, non-number fontSize) into a successful-looking value. The only in-repo caller, updateFontSize (line 20), does `parseSettings(raw)`, mutates fontSize, and calls `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` with no way to tell that parsing failed. Before this change parseSettings threw and updateFontSize aborted before `save`; now, on a corrupt raw string, updateFontSize persists `{"theme":"light","fontSize":size}`, silently discarding the user's stored theme (and any fields) — data loss plus an unrecoverable error signal. As an exported API, parseSettings now forces every caller to conflate 'parse failed' with 'legitimately using defaults'.

findings.whyItBreaks: Pagination page count must cover every item, i.e. ceil(totalItems/pageSize). With Math.floor, any totalItems not evenly divisible by pageSize loses the remainder page. The guard on line 2 only rejects pageSize<=0, so these live inputs reach the changed return and produce a wrong count; the function is an exported public contract whose entire purpose is to bound iteration over all items.

findings.title: buildReport lists artifacts from hardcoded ref, not builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The report's `builtFrom` is resolved from the requested `branch` (line 12: `build.ref(branch)`), but `artifacts` is now resolved from a hardcoded `build.ref("verified")` (line 13) instead of that same `commit`. Whenever the `verified` ref differs from the branch tip — and it does for any branch other than literally "verified" — `buildReport` returns artifacts that do not belong to the commit it advertises. Consumers cannot tell that `artifacts` and `builtFrom` refer to different commits, so a build report can attribute the wrong artifacts to a branch/commit. Secondary consequence: previously `artifactsAt` was always called with a ref derived from the caller-supplied branch; now it depends on a "verified" ref existing in the Build implementation, changing the function from always-succeeding to potentially failing/empty for builds that have no such ref.

findings.title: buildReport returns artifacts from a different commit than builtFrom

The new code resolves a separate hardcoded ref `build.ref("verified")` and returns `artifactsAt(verified)` while leaving `builtFrom: commit` (the branch commit). Every consumer that pairs `builtFrom` with `artifacts` (e.g. to report which commit's artifacts shipped) now gets artifacts from an unrelated revision, and the caller-supplied `branch` argument is silently ignored for the artifacts list. If the `verified` ref does not exist for a given Build implementation, `build.ref("verified")` may also throw or return an unexpected value, breaking the previously working path.

findings.title: Report pairs branch commit with artifacts from "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(build, branch) resolves `commit = build.ref(branch)` and keeps `builtFrom: commit`, but now fetches `artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified)` where `verified = build.ref("verified")`. The `branch` argument no longer affects which artifacts are returned, and the returned `artifacts` are not the artifacts at `builtFrom`. Any consumer that trusts `builtFrom` as the provenance of `artifacts` (e.g. showing "artifacts built from <commit>", cache-keying on builtFrom, or verifying artifact/commit correspondence) receives a self-inconsistent report: artifacts from the `verified` ref labeled as built from the branch commit. Previously both fields referred to the same commit, so this is a regression on every non-`verified` branch.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores positive limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The base returned `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the head replaces the slice with `return sorted;`, so for any limit > 0 the function returns the entire reversed array instead of at most `limit` items. Caller renderFeed(src/feed.ts:9) passes limit=20 and then copies `page.length` items into `out` (src/feed.ts:10-11); with all.length > 20 that loop writes out[20..], growing the array past its allocated size, so renderFeed returns the full feed rather than a 20-entry page. The unchanged doc comment on line 1 ("Returns at most `limit` entries") is now false.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps to limit; returns all entries

The head body computes `const sorted = [...all].reverse()`, returns `[]` only when `limit <= 0`, and otherwise returns `sorted` unchanged — the `.slice(0, limit)` was dropped. For any `limit > 0` the function now returns every entry (reversed) instead of at most `limit`, contradicting the public doc comment 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.' @src/feed.ts:1. The sole caller `renderFeed` @src/feed.ts:9 relies on that promise: it pre-sizes `const out = new Array<string>(20)` @src/feed.ts:10, but its loop `for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i]` @src/feed.ts:11 writes past index 19 when `page.length > 20`, extending `out` to `page.length` elements. So with more than 20 input entries, `renderFeed` returns the entire reversed list instead of a 20-item page — an unbounded user-facing feed.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit > 0 and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The function's doc (line 1) promises "at most `limit` entries, newest first", but the new body builds the reversed array and returns it unmodified whenever limit > 0; only the limit<=0 case is handled. Substituting limit=20: page = all entries reversed, page.length = all.length, so the loop writes past index 20 and renderFeed returns more than the intended 20 entries (JS arrays extend on assignment). The cap that both functions advertise is silently dropped.

findings.whyItBreaks: This line changes backoff()'s unit from seconds (base: Math.min(30, 2**attempt), max 30) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000), max 30_000). src/net/poll.ts was updated to drop its `* 1000`, keeping that caller equivalent, but the other unchanged caller src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. That now sleeps up to 30_000 * 1000 = 30_000_000 ms (~8.33 hours) per attempt instead of the previous max 30 * 1000 = 30_000 ms (30s) — a 1000x regression that effectively hangs any retried job after the first few failures (attempt>=5 reaches the cap).

findings.title: backoff unit change breaks unchanged retry.ts caller (1000x delay)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (2**attempt*1000, capped 30_000 ms), and poll.ts was updated to pass the value directly. But src/jobs/retry.ts:12 is unchanged and still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, re-applying the seconds->ms conversion. retry's sleep becomes 1000x the intended delay: attempt 0 sleeps 1_000*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and attempt 5+ sleeps 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Any caller relying on bounded retry (e.g. job/request paths) will appear hung and likely exceed outer deadlines.

findings.title: backoff() now returns ms but retry.ts still multiplies by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() was changed from returning seconds (min(30, 2**attempt)) to returning milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)). src/net/poll.ts:4 was updated to drop its `* 1000`, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 was not: `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. Substituting the new value: attempt 0 -> min(30000,1000)*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (1,000 s); attempt 1 -> 2,000,000 ms (2,000 s); attempt 2 -> 4,000,000 ms (4,000 s); attempt 5+ -> 30,000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms = 30,000 s (~8.33 h) per retry. Retryable jobs effectively hang instead of retrying on the intended exponential-second schedule (previously capped at 30 s), a severe user-facing regression.

findings.title: Don't swallow os.File.Close error in exported Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Base save.go returned f.Close()'s error to the caller (base line 24). Head adds `defer f.Close()` at line 13, whose return value is discarded, and line 20 returns only w.Flush()'s error. bufio.Writer.Flush hands the bytes to the kernel but the final close(2) can still report delayed write failures (e.g. ENOSPC/EIO on NFS or a failed flush on close); that signal is now lost. Because Save is exported, every caller is forced to treat a close failure as a successful persist, so partially-written data can be reported as saved.

findings.title: Do not discard Close error when saving the file
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code returned the final `f.Close()` error to the caller (base line 20), so a close-time write/flush failure (e.g. delayed-allocation ENOSPC, EIO on NFS, deferred writeback error) surfaced as a non-nil error from Save. The new code defers `f.Close()` (line 13) and returns only `w.Flush()` (line 20); the deferred Close return value is evaluated and thrown away, so the caller receives nil and treats the save as successful even though data may not have been persisted. The failure signal and the success value are now indistinguishable at every caller of this exported function.

findings.title: Save() silently drops f.Close() error via defer
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the file's Close error was returned to the caller (`return f.Close()` at base store/save.go:24, and `f.Close()` before each early return). The new `defer f.Close()` (store/save.go:13) discards that error, and the function now returns only `w.Flush()` (store/save.go:20). For files opened for writing, buffered data and filesystem/metadata errors are frequently surfaced only at Close (e.g. delayed-allocation/writeback, NFS/FUSE, ENOSPC after the final write). In those cases w.Flush() succeeds (it only flushes the userspace bufio buffer into the OS) while f.Close() fails; Save now returns nil, and a caller treats a partially persisted/durability-failed file as a successful save. This is an exported API, so the unusable contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (range off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but page_window iterates range(start, end - 1), excluding the final row of every page. Base code used range(start, end). Substituting rows=[1,2,3,4,5], page_size=2: page 0 start=0,end=2 -> range(0,1) returns [1] instead of [1,2]; page 1 start=2,end=4 -> range(2,3) returns [3] instead of [3,4]; page 2 start=4,end=5 -> range(4,4) returns [] instead of [5]. Both public consumers are affected: render_page @lib/pagination.py:40 renders the truncated window, and summarize @lib/pagination.py:52 concatenates them, so one row per page (and the entire final page when it is full/last) is silently omitted from user-visible output. Row numbering also skips the dropped index (e.g. "1." then "3.").

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (range end - 1)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) (docstring line 18; start=page_index*page_size, end=min(start+page_size,row_count), lines 19-20). The loop must iterate start..end-1 inclusive, i.e. range(start, end). The new code uses range(start, end - 1), which stops one element early, so the final row of every page is omitted. Example: rows=['a','b','c','d'], page_size=3 -> page 0 returns ['a','b'] (drops 'c'); page 1 start=3,end=4 -> range(3,3) is empty (drops 'd' entirely). With page_size=1, end=start+1 so range(start,start) is empty for every page, rendering blank pages. Base code at ff3c797 line 19 used range(start, end), so this is a regression introduced by this PR. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) consume page_window and thus propagate the dropped rows to user-visible output.

findings.title: page_window range(end-1) drops last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns the half-open bounds [start, end) where end = min(start + page_size, row_count) (lib/pagination.py:17-21). The base version iterated `range(start, end)`, collecting every row in the page. The PR changed it to `range(start, end - 1)`, so each page collects only end-start-1 rows and always omits its final row. Concrete substitution: rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_size=2 -> page_count=3; page 0 range(0,1) yields [a] (expected [a,b]), page 1 range(2,3) yields [c] (expected [c,d]), page 2 range(4,4) yields [] (expected [e]). Because render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) consumes this window, summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) joins these truncated pages and rows b, d, e are never emitted. render_page numbering also skips indices (1., 3., 5.) since it counts page_index*page_size while the window shrank. This is a silent data-loss regression on the public output path.

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns expired entries and deletes fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness test was inverted. Previously `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` returned the value only while still within TTL. Now `> this.ttlMs` returns the value exactly when it is EXPIRED, and falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null` for entries that are still fresh. So a cache read after TTL hands back stale data, while any read within TTL evicts the entry and reports a miss — inverting the entire TTL contract of the class.

findings.title: pruneDone skips done jobs due to splice-during-forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: `jobs.splice(index, 1)` shifts every later element down while `forEach` keeps advancing its index, so the element immediately after a removed one is never visited. Example: `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]` → index 0 removes the first, the array becomes `[done,done?]`… concretely `[done,notdone]`, and index 1 now points at `notdone`, leaving a done job in the result. The function no longer prunes all done jobs as its name promises.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's input array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new filtered array and left `jobs` untouched. The new body calls `jobs.splice(...)` and returns the same reference, so any caller holding the original array sees its elements removed as a side effect. Code that keeps the source list (e.g. for retries, logging, or re-pruning) will silently observe a mutated/emptied array, and aliasing bugs appear where callers expect value semantics.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverted comparison serves expired values
findings.whyItBreaks: Base compared `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` and returned the value only while fresh, deleting + returning null once expired. The change to `>` reverses every case: a fresh entry (age < ttlMs) now falls through to `entries.delete(key); return null` at src/cache.ts:21-22, so live data is dropped; an expired entry (age > ttlMs) now returns `entry.value` at src/cache.ts:19 and is never invalidated. Every get() returns the opposite of the intended TTL semantics, so callers serve stale/expired values indefinitely.

findings.title: pruneDone splice-during-forEach skips jobs and mutates caller array
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `jobs.filter((job) => !job.done)` with `forEach` + `jobs.splice(index, 1)` introduces two defects. (1) Splicing shifts the array while forEach advances its index, so adjacent done jobs are skipped: [done,done,done] -> index 0 splices to [done,done], forEach moves to index 1 and splices to [done], loop ends, returning [done] with a done job still present. (2) It mutates the caller's `jobs` array in place and returns the same reference, whereas the previous filter returned a new array and left the input untouched — any caller that reuses its original array now observes it emptied/reordered.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison returns expired cache entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness test was inverted from `<` to `>`. An entry is fresh when `Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs`; with `>` the branch taken for a FRESH entry falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null`, so every unexpired key is dropped on first read. Conversely an EXPIRED entry (`age > ttlMs`) now satisfies the condition and `return entry.value`, so stale values are served forever and never evicted. This is a total inversion of the cache contract: fresh reads miss (and self-delete), expired reads hit.

findings.title: splice inside forEach skips adjacent done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Mutating the array with `splice(index, 1)` while `forEach` is iterating shifts every subsequent element down by one; `forEach` still advances its internal index, so the element immediately after a removed one is never visited. Concrete: `pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true}])` — at index 0 the first job is spliced, the array becomes length 1, the callback next runs at index 1 which no longer exists, and the function returns `[{done:true}]`. The function fails to prune exactly the runs of consecutive done jobs it is named to remove, whereas the previous `filter` removed all of them.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates caller-owned array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `pruneDone(jobs: Job[]): Job[]` previously returned a new filtered array and left the caller's array untouched. The new body calls `jobs.splice(...)` and returns the same reference, so any caller that still holds the original array (e.g. to retry, log, or compare) silently loses entries it did not ask to remove. Return type and name are unchanged, so callers cannot detect the aliasing/mutation from the signature.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN on empty input after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version had `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;`. With that removed, an empty array yields total=0 and rows.length=0, so line 8 computes 0/0 = NaN. Any caller that feeds an empty row set now gets NaN instead of 0, and NaN silently poisons downstream arithmetic/comparisons (e.g. sums, averages, filters) with no error thrown.

findings.title: busiest sorts caller's array in place instead of a copy
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used `const ranked = [...rows].sort(...)` which left the caller's array untouched. The new `rows.sort(...)` sorts the array in place, reordering the caller's data as a side effect. Any caller that reuses its rows array after calling busiest (e.g. displays them in insertion order, paginates, or passes them elsewhere) observes a mutated, reordered array.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was removed. For an empty array the reduce total is 0 and the return is `0 / 0`, which is NaN, not the previous 0. Every caller that expected a numeric 0 for the no-rows case now receives NaN, which silently propagates through arithmetic, comparisons (all false), and JSON serialization (becomes null). This is a behavior regression on a public exported function.

findings.title: busiest() mutates caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The defensive copy `[...rows].sort(...)` was replaced with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place, so busiest() now reorders the caller's array as a side effect. Any caller that relies on its row order after calling busiest() (e.g. rendering, pagination, later averaging/aggregation) silently sees reordered data. The function's contract of returning the single busiest row did not imply mutation of the input.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was removed. For an empty array, reduce returns the initial value 0, then `0 / 0` evaluates to NaN. NaN propagates silently through any downstream sum/compare, serializes to null in JSON, and makes all subsequent arithmetic wrong, whereas the function previously returned 0. This is a changed line (line 8) and a real behavior regression on an exported API.

findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array in place; restore copy
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the array in place, so a read-only query now reorders the caller-owned `rows` array as a side effect. Previously `[...rows].sort(...)` left the input untouched. Any caller that reuses the same array (iterating in original order, rendering rows, or computing a second statistic) now observes a different order than before — a silent data mutation regression introduced on this changed line.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces each number to a string and sorts lexicographically, then reverse() gives string-descending order, not numeric-descending. The base code used scores.sort((a,b)=>b-a). topPlayers reads scores[Math.min(n,scores.length)-1] as the cutoff, so the cutoff is now a string-ranked value. Substitute players=[{name:'a',score:2},{name:'b',score:9},{name:'c',score:10}], n=2: base ranks [10,9,2] and cutoff=9, returning scores {9,10}; head sorts ['10','2','9'] -> reverse ['9','2','10'] and cutoff=2, filter >=2 admits all three in original order, slice(0,2) returns scores {2,9}, silently dropping the 100% legitimate top player (score 10). Because filter preserves input order rather than score order, a too-low cutoff lets earlier low-score players crowd out a true top-n member.

findings.title: rankScores uses lexicographic sort, corrupting topPlayers cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator coerces numbers to strings and sorts lexicographically; `reverse()` then yields descending *string* order, not numeric order. The PR replaced the numeric comparator `(a,b)=>b-a`. Concrete case: players=[{score:2},{score:10}], n=1. rankScores -> [2,10].sort() -> [10,2] ('10'<'2'), reverse -> [2,10], cutoff=scores[0]=2. filter p.score>=2 keeps both, slice(0,1) returns the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player. Any scores spanning digit-length boundaries (9 vs 10, 100 vs 99) mis-rank, so the cutoff can exclude the true top scorer or admit lower ones.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and orders by UTF-16 code units, so multi-digit scores sort lexicographically (e.g. "10" < "11" < "9"). After reverse(), rankScores returns a descending order that is not numeric, so the cutoff at line 15 (scores[min(n,len)-1]) is wrong and too low. topPlayers then keeps the first n players in ORIGINAL array order whose score >= that cutoff, selecting the wrong players. Concrete: players=[{a,9},{b,10},{c,11}], n=1 -> sort gives [10,11,9], reverse [9,11,10], cutoff=9, filter all >=9 in original order, slice(0,1) returns {a,9}; expected the top scorer {c,11}. Also breaks on negatives ("-5" > "-10" lexicographically) and decimals.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used hmac.compare_digest, a constant-time comparison designed to resist timing side channels. Replacing it with the `==` string operator makes verification short-circuit on the first differing byte, leaking how many leading bytes of the expected digest match. An attacker submitting forged signatures can measure response timing to recover the correct HMAC byte-by-byte and ultimately bypass the signature check that gates handle() (app/webhook.py:14). This is CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy) and a direct regression in an authentication path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaced `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Python string `==` short-circuits on the first differing character, so comparison time depends on how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied `given_signature` match the expected digest. An attacker who can send many requests and measure latency can recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and forge a valid signature, bypassing the 401 gate in `handle()` at app/webhook.py:14. `compare_digest` exists specifically to avoid this; the base revision used it correctly.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously compared the computed HMAC against the caller-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest, which is constant-time. The new `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` uses Python's short-circuiting string equality, which returns as soon as the first mismatching byte is found. An attacker who can submit many webhook requests and observe response latency (the 401 vs 200 branch in handle() @app/webhook.py:14) gains a byte-by-byte timing oracle and can recover a valid signature for arbitrary payloads, bypassing the webhook authentication entirely. This is the exact vulnerability class hmac.compare_digest exists to prevent.

findings.title: Balance updates now run outside the transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs all executed inside `with db.transaction():`, so the transfer was all-or-nothing. The refactor only wraps `_record_ledger(...)` in the transaction (app/transfer.py:22-23) and calls `_apply_balances(...)` after the `with` block exits (app/transfer.py:24). The ledger row is therefore committed in one transaction, and the two balance UPDATEs run in a separate (implicit/autocommit) transaction. If `_apply_balances` raises — DB error, constraint failure, lost connection, process crash — the ledger already records a completed transfer while neither account balance changed, leaving the ledger and balances permanently inconsistent with no rollback. Even the two UPDATEs themselves are no longer atomic relative to each other (debit can commit while credit fails).

findings.title: Balance updates escaped the transaction; transfer is no longer atomic
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside the single `with db.transaction():` block (base lines 4-15), so any failure rolled all three back. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the transaction (line 23); `_apply_balances` (line 24) runs after the `with` exits, i.e. outside the transaction/commit boundary. If the second UPDATE fails (constraint/DB error, crash, or connection drop) or the process dies between the commit and the updates, the ledger permanently records a transfer whose balances were never changed, or — if the first UPDATE commits independently (autocommit) — the source is debited without the destination being credited. That is lost/corrupted financial state, the exact case the original transaction guarded.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the refactor all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction()`, so they committed or rolled back together. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (line 23); `_apply_balances` is called after the `with` block exits (line 24), so the ledger row commits first and the two balance UPDATEs execute outside any transaction. If the process dies, the DB connection drops, or the first/second UPDATE raises between line 23 and line 24, the ledger records a transfer whose balances were never (or only partially) applied — money is effectively created/destroyed and the ledger and account balances permanently disagree. This is a regression introduced by this PR, not pre-existing behavior.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, shifting day boundaries by server TZ
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation computed the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, giving a timezone-independent (UTC) billing day. The new line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the host's local timezone. The returned string now changes with the server's TZ env/config: e.g. 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z under TZ=America/New_York yields "2023-12-31" instead of "2024-01-01". This mis-assigns charges to the wrong billing day and makes sameBillingDay (line 8) return true/false based on local offset. Results also differ between two servers/processes in different timezones processing the same timestamp.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, not UTC, shifting billing dates
findings.whyItBreaks: Base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; this line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. The output format is unchanged, but the value now depends on the runtime's local timezone. For any timestamp whose local date differs from its UTC date (e.g. 2024-01-01T23:30:00Z on a UTC-negative host, or 2024-01-01T01:00:00Z on a UTC-positive host), billingDay() returns a different day than before. Because sameBillingDay() (line 8) compares billingDay() results, billing-period equality also flips for those timestamps. The same Date now maps to different billing days depending on the server's TZ setting, and the date can change across a deploy/migration to a differently-configured host, causing misattributed billing-day buckets.

findings.title: billingDay uses local time, breaking timezone-stable billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR billingDay derived Y-M-D from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so the billing-day key was a property of the instant and identical on every host. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the key now depends on the runtime's local timezone (and shifts across DST). Two servers in different zones (or the same server before/after a TZ or DST change) will map the same instant to different billing days, and two instants that are the same UTC day can map to different local days. sameBillingDay() at line 8 compares these strings, so day-equality and any billing period keyed on it can now disagree, causing split or duplicated billing windows.

findings.title: Restore tenant in cache key to stop cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is keyed only by `account` now. `readProfile(tenant, account)` promises a tenant-scoped Profile (params at src/profile.ts:10-11; Profile carries its own `tenant` at src/profile.ts:2), but the cache lookup at line 15 and the write at line 18 no longer distinguish tenants. First caller for account 'alice' (e.g. tenant 'A') populates the cache; a later call `readProfile('B', 'alice')` hits the cache and returns tenant A's Profile object — including `profile.tenant === 'A'` and A's `displayName` — to tenant B without ever invoking `fetchProfile('B','alice')`. This is a cross-tenant data-leak / wrong-profile regression introduced by this PR; previously the `${tenant}:${account}` key prevented it.

findings.title: Restore tenant in cache key to prevent cross-tenant profile leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` (line 7) is keyed only by `account` now. `readProfile(tenant, account)` promises to return the profile for that tenant+account, but the lookup at line 15 and write at line 18 ignore `tenant`. If tenant A fetches account 'alice', the profile is cached under 'alice'; a later call for tenant B with the same account name hits `memo.get('alice')`, returns tenant A's Profile at line 16, and never calls `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` (line 17). This silently serves one tenant's profile to another tenant and skips the per-tenant fetch — a cross-tenant data disclosure, not merely a cache miss.

findings.title: Restore tenant in profile cache key to prevent cross-tenant leak
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level `Map<string, Profile>` (src/profile.ts:7) shared across all calls. Changing `key` from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` makes the cache tenant-agnostic: after `readProfile('tenantA','alice',...)` populates the map, a later `readProfile('tenantB','alice',...)` hits `if (cached) return cached` (src/profile.ts:16) and returns tenantA's profile without ever calling `fetchProfile(tenantB,'alice')`. The function signature still promises a tenant-scoped profile (src/profile.ts:9-13) and the returned `Profile` carries a `tenant` field, so callers receive another tenant's account data — a tenant-isolation/confidentiality violation.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error as empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: before this PR, load() threw `missing: <key>` on an absent key and loadAll() propagated that throw. Now the catch-all maps the failure to the string "", which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty value. Every caller (including the in-repo loadAll at src/store.ts:12, which maps keys through load and returns the array) can no longer detect a missing key — it receives a real-looking "" and may act on/persist it as if the key existed. Because load is an exported public function, the unusable contract ships now regardless of current callers.

findings.title: Stop swallowing missing-key error in load(); it hides failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all discards the `Error(`missing: ${key}`)` signal and returns "". `store` is `Map<string,string>`, so "" is a legitimate stored value; every caller can no longer tell 'key absent' from 'key mapped to empty string'. Previously a missing key threw and forced the caller to handle it. `loadAll` (the only in-repo caller) now silently returns "" array elements for missing keys instead of propagating, so callers that treat the result as real data will read an empty value as if it were stored config. `load` is exported, so this is also a broken public contract for every future caller.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when the key was absent; callers could rely on the throw to detect a missing entry. The new catch-all block converts that failure into "", an ordinary value. Any caller (including the exported loadAll at src/store.ts:11-13) now receives "" for a missing key, indistinguishable from a key that genuinely stores an empty string, so missing-data conditions are silently treated as real empty data (TRIGGER D). The bare `catch {}` also swallows any error thrown by store.get, further erasing the failure signal.

findings.title: Renaming exported Config.timeoutMs to timeout breaks consumers
findings.whyItBreaks: base had `timeoutMs: number` on the exported Config interface; this hunk removes it and adds `timeout: number`, and line 8/21 now read `config.timeout`. TypeScript consumers passing `{maxAttempts, timeoutMs}` fail to compile; untyped/JS consumers keep passing `timeoutMs`, so `config.timeout` is undefined, `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN`, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` @10/@23 is always false — the timeout is silently disabled and the function retries maxAttempts/retries times with no deadline. The rename also drops the explicit `Ms` unit while the body still adds the value to `Date.now()` (milliseconds).

findings.title: retryBackground uses `retries` as total attempts; retries:0 never calls fn
findings.whyItBreaks: The field name `retries` (line 3) promises a count of retries (total attempts = retries + 1), but the loop body `for (let i = 0; i < config.retries; i++)` treats it as the total attempt count. Substituting the common value `retries: 0` ('no extra retries, try once') yields zero iterations, so `fn()` is never invoked and `retryBackground` returns normally with no work done and no error. `retries: 1` likewise performs one attempt instead of an initial try plus one retry, diverging from the name and from `retry`'s `maxAttempts` semantics in the same shared Config type.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function wraps `fn()` in `try { ... } catch { continue; }` and returns `void`. After all attempts fail, the last error is discarded and the caller receives no signal distinguishing 'succeeded' from 'failed after N attempts'; a caller cannot know whether to persist, report, or compensate. Absent this catch-all the thrown error would propagate to the caller, so the swallow is the changed behavior. As an exported public API it forces every eventual caller to conflate failure with success.

findings.title: Revert breaking rename timeoutMs→timeout on exported Config

Renaming the field to `timeout` (and making `retries` a required member) breaks every existing caller of the exported API. A TypeScript caller no longer satisfies the interface (build break); an untyped/JS caller keeps passing `timeoutMs`, so `config.timeout` is `undefined`, `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is `NaN` at line 8, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` (line 10) is `Date.now() > NaN` → always false. Separately, `retries` is now required on the shared Config even though `retry` never reads it, forcing existing `retry` callers to supply an unused field.

findings.title: retryBackground discards every failure and returns success
findings.whyItBreaks: The added exported function catches every error from `fn()` and `continue`s, then falls off the end returning `void`. There is no return value, no rethrow, and no log, so a caller cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded on some attempt' from 'fn failed on all attempts'. Because the only failure signal (the thrown exception) is discarded, every caller is forced to treat a total failure as a success; acting on that (marking work done, advancing a queue, reporting success) is wrong. This is the public API contract itself, independent of any current caller.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the deadline guard

The deadline branch therefore never fires and `retry` loops up to `maxAttempts` with no time limit — the timeout behavior that existed before this PR is gone.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all errors and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly exported retryBackground catches every error with a bare `catch { continue; }` and returns `void`. If every attempt fails it exits normally with no thrown error, no return value, and no log. findings.title: Do not call .length on string|number union value

findings.title: Workflow echoes secret TOKEN into CI logs

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step exports secrets.TOKEN into the environment and prints it with `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, so the credential is written to the job log on every push (workflow triggers `on: push`, line 2). Anyone with log read access — including all repo collaborators, and the public in a public repo — can retrieve it via the web UI or the logs API. GitHub's automatic masking is best-effort and only covers the exact secret string; it is bypassed by any transformation (encoding, substring, whitespace) and does not remove the secret from downloaded logs. The token is never used for any build/deploy action here, so there is zero functional justification for the exposure.
