findings.title: Bundle baseSha no longer matches reviewed diff range
findings.whyItBreaks: The reviewed content is computed from mergeBase: patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) at line 140 and changedFiles = changedFileSet(cwd, mergeBase) at line 141. The bundle, however, now reports baseSha (the live PR base-branch tip from PR_BASE_SHA, line 138) instead of mergeBase. Any consumer of bundle.baseSha that re-derives or displays the range (e.g. re-running git diff baseSha headSha or resolving base-side file contents) inspects a different range than what was reviewed: a two-dot diff against the base tip pulls in unrelated commits that landed on the base branch after the PR branched and can misattribute/miss PR changes. The declared base is now inconsistent with the patch it ships.

findings.title: Removing git maxBuffer aborts review on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's spawnSync default maxBuffer is ~1 MiB. The git helper is used for `git diff mergeBase headSha` at line 140 (and changedFileSet's `diff --name-only`). On a moderately large PR that output exceeds the cap, spawnSync returns status=null with error.code=ENOBUFS; the guard `if (res.status !== 0)` (line 38) then throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty stderr, aborting the review before it runs. The sibling gh/ghText helpers still pass 64 MiB, so only git is affected. Reproduced on this host: spawning a 2,000,000-byte producer with encoding utf8 yields status=null, error.code=ENOBUFS.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer; >1MB PR diffs now abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the `git()` spawnSync, so Node's default maxBuffer (1024*1024 = 1 MiB) applies. When stdout exceeds it, spawnSync terminates git, sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null, with truncated stdout/stderr. `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` at line 140 is the exact call that can exceed 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, large PRs). The guard `res.status !== 0` (null !== 0) then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with empty stderr, the catch at line 182 posts a failure check and sets exit code 1 — the entire review aborts for any PR whose diff is >1 MiB. The sibling `gh` helpers (lines 19, 29) and the canonical `runText` (src/shared/process.ts:16 in the upstream tree) still cap at 64 MiB, confirming the limit was intentional.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha no longer matches the patch's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: `patch` (line 140) and `changedFiles` (line 141) are both computed from `mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha)`, but the bundle now advertises `baseSha` (the PR base tip from PR_BASE_SHA / origin/main). Whenever the base branch has advanced past the PR fork point, `baseSha !== mergeBase`, so the bundle's declared base is inconsistent with the diff it carries: consumers that use `bundle.baseSha` to describe or reconstruct the review target (the `{{BASE}}` substitution and `ReviewResult.baseSha` in the review core) advertise a base whose diff against head includes unrelated base-branch commits, not the patch that was actually reviewed. The previous `baseSha: mergeBase` was the value consistent with patch/changedFiles, and every other adapter path (e.g. upstream src/adapters/github.ts:894, src/shared/repo.ts prDiffFromShas) uses the merge base.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git(): large diffs now fail or truncate
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the only large-output path: `const patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` (line 140) captures the entire PR diff. Dropping `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` falls back to Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB. For any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB (lockfiles, generated files, big refactors), spawnSync sets res.error (ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER) and res.status becomes null, so `res.status !== 0` at line 38 is true and the function throws `git diff ... failed:` (with empty stderr because res.error is never read). runGithub then posts a 'review failed' check and exits 1 — a PR that previously reviewed fine now hard-fails. Even if a Node version returned status 0 with truncated stdout, the reviewer would silently receive an incomplete patch. gh() (line 19) and ghText() (line 29) still pass 64 MiB, confirming the git() removal is inconsistent.

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha no longer matches the base of bundle.patch
findings.whyItBreaks: `patch` and `changedFiles` are computed from `mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseSha, headSha])` (lines 139-141), but the bundle now reports the raw `baseSha` from PR_BASE_SHA / `merge-base origin/main HEAD` (line 138) instead of `mergeBase`. When the PR base is not an ancestor of head (base branch advanced, or PR_BASE_SHA is the branch tip), mergeBase != baseSha, so the declared base no longer describes the diff it is shipped with. review(bundle) (line 177) and any consumer that resolves base-side content via `git show <baseSha>:<path>` or `git diff <baseSha> <headSha>` will see a different changeset than `patch` — including unrelated commits already on the base branch — producing misleading context/findings. The mature version of this adapter keeps the invariant `baseSha: mergeBase` (cross-checked in sibling copies: /tmp/needlefish-1161-budget/src/adapters/github.ts:896 and /tmp/needlefish-self-managed-workflows-20260908/src/adapters/github.ts:896), which confirms mergeBase is the intended value.

findings.title: Re-add `-s read-only`; removing it lets codex mutate the repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns the `codex` agentic CLI with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (src/shared/codex.ts:24) and feeds it an externally supplied prompt. The removed `-s read-only` flag was a hard override that forced the sandbox to read-only for model-generated shell commands regardless of any user/project Codex config. With it gone, the effective sandbox is now whatever `~/.codex/config.toml` / project config (or the CLI default) specifies, so the agent can request/perform writes inside the repo under review and run non-read-only commands. For a review tool whose job is to read a diff and emit JSON, that is a security/supply-chain downgrade (arbitrary repo mutation, destructive command execution) with no functional benefit — `--output-last-message` is written by codex itself and is unaffected by the sandbox.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: `-s read-only` was the only sandbox enforcement in this function. With the flag removed, `codex exec` (src/shared/codex.ts:23-29) inherits the host config's sandbox mode. On this host ~/.codex/config.toml sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`, so the agent invoked with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and `input: prompt` (prompt is derived from untrusted PR content) runs with unrestricted filesystem write, network, and command execution and no approval prompts. A prompt-injected diff can therefore exfiltrate secrets, modify/corrupt the repo under review, or execute arbitrary commands during a review — the exact confinement the explicit flag existed to guarantee. Even absent that host config, the change moves the security guarantee from code into ambient, potentially permissive configuration.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox pin for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `-s read-only` from the `codex exec` argv. `codex exec` loads `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (default `~/.codex/config.toml`) unless `--ignore-user-config` is passed, and `-s` has no CLI default, so the sandbox mode is now resolved entirely from ambient config/env. On this host `~/.codex/config.toml` lines 1-2 set `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`; previously the explicit flag overrode that and forced read-only. Consequently `runCodex` spawns codex with unrestricted host filesystem/network write access and no approval prompts, while the prompt includes untrusted repository/diff content (prompt-injection surface). Codex can then modify the host or exfiltrate secrets instead of merely reading the reviewed repo.

findings.title: Diff from base tip, not merge base, pulls non-PR changes into review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the reviewed range was `merge-base(baseSha, headSha) .. headSha`; now it is `baseSha .. HEAD`. `baseSha = process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || git merge-base origin/main HEAD` (line 138). When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch tip (its intended usage) and the base branch advanced after the PR forked, `baseSha` is NOT an ancestor of the PR head, so the two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 139) and `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (line 57, called at line 140) include every base-branch commit made after the fork, i.e. files the PR never touched. Consequences: (a) the model reviews code that is not part of the PR; (b) `changedPaths` (line 141) becomes a superset, and `inlineComments` filters findings by `changedPaths.has(f.file)` (line 63), so a finding on a base-branch-only file is sent as an inline comment on a line absent from the PR diff — GitHub rejects the review and the catch at line 86 silently reposts body-only, dropping all inline comments; (c) the diff also targets the working-tree `HEAD` instead of the resolved `headSha`, so under Actions' default `pull_request` checkout (`refs/pull/N/merge`) HEAD is the synthetic merge commit, making the reviewed patch inconsistent with the `headSha` the review is posted against (lines 178/180).

findings.title: Use merge-base, not base tip, for PR patch and changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed code computed `mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha` and reviewed `git diff mergeBase headSha` (a three-dot PR diff). The new code does a two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)`. Two-dot diffs compare the base branch tip directly, so once the base branch advances after the PR branched, the patch and changedFiles include commits that are NOT part of the PR. Because this adapter reads files from the working tree and posts `commit_id: headSha` (line 137/150), the working tree must be the PR head, i.e. HEAD == headSha; in that case unrelated base changes are fed to the reviewer, producing false-positive findings/changes_requested and misclassified changed files. Findings on those unrelated files also pass the `changedPaths` filter (line 63), so inline comments can target lines not present in the PR diff; GitHub then rejects the review POST and the unchanged `catch` at line 96 silently falls back to a comment-only review, dropping all inline findings.

findings.title: Diff PR against merge-base, not raw baseSha..HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: This adapter is the Actions entry point (line 134 requires GITHUB_REPOSITORY). baseSha is the base-branch tip from PR_BASE_SHA (or merge-base(origin/main,HEAD) in the local fallback, line 138), and headSha is PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137). The old code diffed merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha, i.e. only the commits the PR adds on top of the common ancestor. The new code diffs baseSha..HEAD (two-dot). Two concrete wrong effects when the env vars are set: (1) if the base branch advanced after the PR branched, baseSha != merge-base(baseSha,headSha), so the patch and changedFiles include base-only commits shown as reversions (files/changes the PR never touched) and the model reviews a polluted diff; (2) the patch now reads the literal 'HEAD' instead of headSha, and in a default pull_request checkout HEAD is the PR merge commit, while the review is still posted against headSha (postReview commit_id line 178, postCheck head_sha line 179). The reviewed diff therefore need not correspond to the commit being commented on, and inline-comment line numbers derived from changedFiles (lines 61-69) can be mis-anchored or rejected. Result: false findings / spurious REQUEST_CHANGES and mis-posted comments.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to stop $-pattern corruption of prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement interprets special patterns: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched sentinel, `` $` ``→text before the match, `$'`→text after the match. The old code passed `() => ...` (a function replacement), which disables that interpretation. After this change, `JSON.stringify(bundle)` (line 25, which embeds `bundle.patch`), `JSON.stringify(candidate)` (line 32), and `bundle.patch` (line 33) are injected verbatim as replacement strings, so any diff/model text containing those sequences is silently rewritten before being sent to Codex. Example verified with node: `"X {{PATCH}} Y".replace("{{PATCH}}", "cost=$& pid=$$")` yields `"X cost={{PATCH}} pid=$ Y"` (sentinel re-injected, `$$` collapsed), while the function form preserves the text exactly. The patch is arbitrary code under review, so `$&`/`$$`/`$'` occurrences (JS regex replacements, shell scripts, Makefiles) corrupt the critic/review prompt and can produce wrong review output.

findings.title: Restore function-form replace() to stop $ substitution corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace(string, replacement) treats the replacement as a template: $$, $&, $`, $', and $n are special. The base code passed a function `() => ...`, which is returned verbatim, precisely to avoid this. The head passes raw strings: JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2) (line 25), JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2) (line 32), and bundle.patch (line 33). A code diff (bundle.patch) or JSON payload routinely contains `$` (shell vars, template literals, regex, jQuery-style `$`). Any `$` sequence is rewritten or a `{{...}}` placeholder can be re-injected ($& inserts the matched substring), so the review/critic prompt no longer contains the literal bundle/patch. The model is then reviewed on corrupted input, silently degrading/altering the review result. The base used function callbacks, confirming the string form is the regression.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to stop `$` pattern corruption of prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When the replacement argument to String.prototype.replace is a plain string, JS interprets `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$n`, `$<name>` as substitution patterns. The inserted values here are arbitrary user/LLM/diff text (JSON.stringify(bundle) includes bundle.patch, JSON.stringify(candidate) includes finding prose, and bundle.patch is the raw diff), which routinely contain `$` sequences. Verified in this repo: `"x{{PATCH}}y".replace("{{PATCH}}", "$`")` returns `"xxy"` and `"$&"` expands to the matched literal `{{PATCH}}`, so patch content like `$$5` collapses to `$5` and `$&` re-injects the placeholder. The critic therefore reviews a mutated diff and the reviewer a mutated bundle, producing wrong findings/verdicts. The base code deliberately used `() => ...` replacers (see `git show 9926a02:src/core/review.ts`) precisely to insert the text verbatim; this diff removes that protection.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in postReview fallback to pin review to headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's primary call pins the review to the reviewed commit via `commit_id: headSha` (line 89), but the catch fallback now sends only `event` and `body` (lines 107-110). GitHub's create-review endpoint treats commit_id as optional and defaults to the PR's current latest commit, so when the fallback fires (primary POST rejected) the review is attached to whatever commit is currently at the PR head rather than the `headSha` that was actually reviewed. This happens concretely when a workflow run for commit A is re-run after commit B is pushed (PR_HEAD_SHA stays A while the PR head is B) or when a push lands during the review. The check-run is still keyed to `headSha` (line 128 / postCheck call line 184), so the verdict comment and the check disagree and a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT review computed against A's diff is recorded against B, which was never reviewed. Re-adding the field costs nothing and the primary path already sends it.

findings.title: Fallback review loses commit_id, may attach to wrong commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary POST pins the review to the reviewed commit via `commit_id: headSha` (line 89), but the catch-block fallback (lines 101-111) now sends only `event` and `body`. GitHub's create-review API documents `commit_id` as defaulting to "the most recent commit in the pull request when you do not specify a value", so whenever the PR head moves during the run (or `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from the branch head, which the adapter explicitly allows at line 141), the review body rendered from the mergeBase..headSha diff is attached to an unreviewed commit. Meanwhile `postCheck` still pins the check run to `headSha` (line 184), so the review and the required check refer to different commits, and a REQUEST_CHANGES/APPROVE verdict can appear to apply to code that was never analyzed.

findings.title: Stop silently fabricating malformed findings in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body validated every field and threw (`malformed finding: invalid severity`, `missing file`, etc. at base src/shared/schema.ts:101,105,108,110,112,114,117,121); normalizeReview's non-strict mode dropped bad findings via try/catch. Now normalizeFinding never throws, so a garbage entry becomes a real-looking Finding: invalid severity -> `P1`, invalid/missing category -> `bug`, missing file -> `""`, missing title -> `"Untitled finding"`, missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> `""`. normalizeReview removed the `strict` parameter and now always maps every raw finding, so callers can no longer distinguish "the model emitted a malformed finding" from "the model emitted a real P1/bug finding". This is an exported public API, so the unusable contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Line-range fallback emits NaN and non-positive lines
findings.whyItBreaks: `Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0)` only substitutes 0 for null/undefined; a non-numeric value (e.g. "abc", {}, []) yields NaN, and negatives/fractions pass straight through. The old code required `Number.isFinite(lineStart) && lineStart > 0` (base src/shared/schema.ts:115-118) and did the same for lineEnd (base 119-122). The normalized Finding can now carry lineStart/lineEnd of NaN, 0, -1, or 3.7, which breaks the documented replacement contract (`replacement` replaces exactly lineStart..lineEnd) for any consumer.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed input into fake P1 findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, every invalid/missing required field in a model-emitted finding threw and aborted parsing: not-an-object (base 96-98), invalid severity (base 100-102), invalid category (base 104-106), missing file (base 107-108), missing title (base 109-110), missing whyItBreaks (base 111-112), missing suggestedFix (base 113-114), non-finite/<=0 lineStart (base 115-118), non-finite/<=0 lineEnd (base 119-122). Those throws propagated out of normalizeReview via base:156, so callers could tell the review output was malformed. The new body instead maps failure to plausible-looking values: severity -> "P1", category -> "bug", file -> "", title -> "Untitled finding", lineStart/lineEnd -> 0, whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> "". A malformed or hallucinated finding is therefore emitted as a real, high-severity finding with no file/line, indistinguishable from a genuine one, and a P1 can force changes_requested/block a merge. This is a present defect in the exported API contract, not a future-caller concern.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates findings from malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: Every validation that previously rejected malformed findings was replaced by a default: invalid severity -> "P1" (line 98), invalid/missing category -> "bug" (100-102), missing file -> "" (103), missing title -> "Untitled finding" (99), missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> "" (107-108), and lineStart/lineEnd -> Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) (104-105), which yields 0 for absent values and NaN for non-numeric values (e.g. lineStart:"abc" -> NaN, which JSON.stringify serializes as null). A caller can no longer distinguish a real finding from a fabricated one, so a malformed/empty review item is now reported as a legitimate P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0/NaN instead of raising "malformed finding". The base version threw on all of these (base lines 96-122), and normalizeReview's removed `strict` default (base line 137/155) means there is no longer any fail-closed path — the old lenient branch dropped invalid findings, whereas the new body keeps them.

findings.title: Restore -R for gh pr view in pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (line 26) runs BEFORE actions/checkout (line 42), so on a clean/ephemeral self-hosted runner $GITHUB_WORKSPACE has no .git. Without -R, gh tries to infer the repo from the local git remote and exits non-zero ('failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository'); gh does not fall back to GITHUB_REPOSITORY (verified with gh 2.98.0: strings has 0 occurrences of GITHUB_REPOSITORY, and a full Actions-like env still fails). Because the failing command sits inside `$(...)` of an `echo`, bash `-e` does not abort, so the step still succeeds and writes `head=`/`base=` empty; actions/checkout then falls back to the event's default ref and the review runs against the wrong commit. Only the workflow_dispatch path hits this else branch (pull_request sets EVENT_HEAD), so manual reviews are broken/mis-targeted. The removed `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` env (line 29) is required to restore the fix.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in pre-checkout refs step
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (line 26) runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so at that point there is no `.git`/origin remote in the workspace. `gh` resolves the target repo from `-R`/`GH_REPO` or the local git remote only (verified locally: with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set but no git repo, `gh pr view 123 ...` fails `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`; with `GH_REPO` set it resolves). The else branch (lines 37-40) is reached only on `workflow_dispatch`, where `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty. Previously `-R "$REPO"` (env at old line 30) made resolution independent of the workspace. Now `gh pr view` fails; because the failure is inside `echo "head=$(...)"`, bash `-e`/`pipefail` does not abort (verified: `bash -eo pipefail -c 'echo "head=$(false)" >> /dev/null; echo ok'` continues), so the step succeeds while writing `head=` and `base=` empty to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. Checkout then falls back to the dispatched ref instead of the PR head, and the review runs with empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` — i.e. the manual trigger no longer reviews the requested PR.

findings.title: Removing -R $REPO breaks gh pr view in pre-checkout dispatch path
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step (lines 26-40) executes BEFORE `actions/checkout` (lines 42-46). Without `-R "$REPO"`, `gh pr view` determines the repository from the local git remote, not from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`. Verified locally with the installed gh 2.98.0: in a non-git dir `gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`, and even inside a git repo with no remote it fails with `no git remotes found` despite `GITHUB_REPOSITORY=owner/repo` being set. On the workflow_dispatch path `EVENT_HEAD` is empty (github.event.pull_request is null), so the `else` branch runs and both `gh` calls fail; because they are inside `$(...)` in an `echo`, the step still exits 0 and writes `head=`/`base=` empty. The subsequent checkout then uses an empty `ref` and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` are empty, so the review targets the wrong/missing refs. The `pull_request` path is unaffected (it takes the `-n "$EVENT_HEAD"` branch).

findings.title: Restore strict parsing of candidate findings; false drops real findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The second argument to normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) disables strict validation: with strict=false each finding goes through normalizeFinding in a try/catch that returns null on any throw, and null entries are filtered out. normalizeFinding throws on a malformed required field (invalid/missing severity or category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd). The candidate pass is exactly what feeds the critic via {{FINDINGS}} (line 35), and the critic only prunes — it cannot recover a finding already dropped. So a genuine P0/P1/P2 finding with one malformed field is silently removed from candidate.findings, never reaches the critic or the returned pruned.findings, and deriveVerdict (line 42) returns pass instead of changes_requested. The base code called normalizeReview(extractJson(rawCandidate)) with the strict default, so malformed output aborted the review; this call now swallows that failure. The critic pass on line 38 still uses the strict default, making the candidate pass the only lenient one.

findings.title: Candidate parsed with strict=false silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true). With strict=false, each finding is passed through normalizeFinding inside a try/catch and any that throws is mapped to null and filtered out (src/shared/schema.ts:155-165, non-strict branch). The candidate pass is the raw model output, so a real P1/P2 finding with a single malformed required field (missing title/whyItBreaks, invalid severity/category, lineStart<=0) is silently discarded from candidate.findings. The guard on line 30 only checks candidate.summary and candidate.checked, which are still populated, so nothing throws and the loss is invisible. That finding never reaches the critic (line 34-36), so it cannot appear in the final pruned findings and the derived verdict can flip from changes_requested to pass. The critic pass on line 38 still uses the strict default, so only the candidate pass is affected.

findings.title: Parse candidate review strictly so malformed findings aren't dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is declared `normalizeReview(raw: unknown, strict = true)` (src/shared/normalize.ts:181). With the added `false`, the candidate branch takes the lenient path (src/shared/normalize.ts:187-197): each finding is run through normalizeFinding and any throw is caught, mapped to null, and filtered out. Previously the default strict=true propagated that error and aborted the review. The only post-parse guard here (src/core/review.ts:30) checks `candidate.summary` and `candidate.checked.length`, never `candidate.findings`, so a candidate whose finding has one malformed required field (invalid severity, lineEnd < lineStart, non-numeric/low confidence for a P0-P2, missing title) passes with that finding silently removed. The critic prompt is fed `JSON.stringify(candidate, ...)` (src/core/review.ts:35) and prompts/critic.md forbids it from adding new findings, so the dropped P1/P2 is permanently lost and the review can return a false pass.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-review errors into empty pass
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (920b73e) normalizeReview threw `malformed review output: ...` when raw was not an object or summary/findings/checked/residual_risks had the wrong type (base schema.ts:115-131), so a truncated or invalid model response surfaced as a hard failure the caller could retry or escalate. The new body replaces every guard with a default: non-array findings -> [], non-array residual_risks -> [], non-string summary -> "", non-array checked -> []. A caller receiving `{}` (or a response missing the fields because the model was cut off) now gets `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` — byte-for-byte the shape of a legitimate zero-finding review. Because the verdict/`blocks` signal is derived from these arrays (schema.ts:68-73, ResidualRisk.blocks @schema.ts:65), the fallback reads as "nothing found, nothing blocking" rather than "review failed", so a broken review can be reported/merged as a pass. The swallow site is exported (public contract), so every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with an empty review even though there are no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation threw on non-object input and on missing/non-string summary and missing findings/checked/residual_risks arrays. The new body replaces every one of those propagation branches with a default: `Array.isArray(raw?.findings) ? ... : []` (115-117), `Array.isArray(raw?.residual_risks) ? ... : []` (118-123), `String(raw?.summary ?? "")` (125), and `Array.isArray(raw?.checked) ? ... : []` (127). As a result `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview({})`, or `normalizeReview({summary: 123, findings: "oops"})` all return `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` — byte-identical to a legitimately empty review. A caller that treats an empty findings/checked list as a clean pass (the natural reading of this data) can no longer tell that the model returned unusable output, so a failed/truncated response is reported as an approving review instead of surfacing an error. This is a public exported symbol (the only consumer contract in this shared module), so the unusable contract is the defect even with no in-repo caller in this snapshot.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed review output as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version rejected non-object input and missing/typed-out fields by throwing ('malformed review output: ...'), so a failed or non-conforming model response surfaced as an error. The new body uses optional chaining and Array.isArray fallbacks, so normalizeReview(null), normalizeReview(undefined), normalizeReview("garbage"), or an object missing findings/summary/checked/residual_risks now returns { summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] } — a shape indistinguishable from a legitimate clean review. Any consumer that derives a verdict (empty findings + no blocking residual risks ⇒ pass) can no longer tell 'the review never produced valid output' from 'the review found nothing', so malformed output can be silently treated as an approving review. This is an exported function, so the unusable contract is itself the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large diffs fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB (1024*1024). git() is used at line 100 for `git diff <baseSha> HEAD`, whose stdout is the entire patch and routinely exceeds 1 MiB on real PRs (lockfiles, generated files, monorepos). When the cap is exceeded Node kills the child and sets res.error to an ENOBUFS error with res.status=null; line 12 treats null !== 0 as failure and line 13 throws `git diff ... failed: ` using only res.stderr, which is empty for ENOBUFS. The tool's core workflow (review a PR) therefore aborts with an uninformative error for large diffs, a regression from the base's explicit 64 MiB buffer. gh() at line 36 still carries maxBuffer 64 MiB, so the limit is inconsistent within the same file.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync or large diffs fail
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the git helper, leaving Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB (1024*1024). The helper is used for `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` (line 88) and `git diff --name-only` (line 89) in runLocal. When a diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync kills git and sets res.error=ENOBUFS with res.status=null and (typically) empty stderr. The unchanged guard `res.status !== 0` (line 12) then throws `git diff <sha> HEAD failed: ` with an empty detail, and runLocal aborts before any review runs. Previously output up to 64 MiB was accepted, so this is a user-facing regression on exactly the large PRs the tool exists to review; the discarded res.error also hides the real cause (ENOBUFS).

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: default 1 MiB truncates git diff, breaks large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used at line 100 as `const patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` to capture the ENTIRE diff into the review bundle. Removing maxBuffer drops spawnSync back to Node's default of ~1 MiB of stdout (verified: spawning a 2 MB writer with no maxBuffer returns status=null, error.code=ENOBUFS). A diff over that size (lockfiles, generated code, vendored deps, broad refactors — normal for this tool's input) makes spawnSync abort with ENOBUFS and status=null; the unchanged guard `res.status !== 0` is then true, so git() throws and runLocal fails before any review runs. Worse, res.stderr is empty on ENOBUFS, so the thrown message is `git diff <sha> HEAD failed: ` with no cause, masking the real reason. The base had maxBuffer=64 MiB precisely to allow large patches.

findings.title: Report failed review as neutral check, letting errored PRs pass
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block, postCheck() now posts the 'Needlefish' check run with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub treats `neutral` as a non-blocking/passing conclusion for required status checks, so when review() throws, the review gate no longer blocks the PR even though the summary at line 193 explicitly says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.' `process.exitCode = 1` only fails the Actions job; it does not change the conclusion of the separately-created 'Needlefish' check run that branch protection may require. The result is that an errored review can be merged as if it passed.

findings.title: Errored review now posts non-blocking neutral check
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block that handles a failed review changed the check-run conclusion from "failure" to "neutral" (line 191), while the check summary on line 193 still states `Review errored and did NOT pass this PR`. GitHub treats `neutral` as passing for required status checks, so a PR whose review errored can now be merged despite the check text claiming it did not pass. Previously (`git show 9238431:src/adapters/github.ts`) this path passed "failure", which blocks a required check. The `process.exitCode = 1` on line 196 only fails the Actions step; the dedicated check run named "Needlefish" (line 187-194) is what branch protection reads, and it is now green/neutral.

findings.title: gh pr diff ignores runGithub cwd, may diff wrong repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `ghText` (lines 28-34) spawns `gh` without a `cwd` option, and `gh pr diff <N>` is repository-implicit: it resolves the repo from the child process's working directory (or GH_REPO/-R). The replaced call `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` was explicitly scoped to the `cwd` argument, and every other git operation still is. If runGithub is invoked with a `cwd` that differs from `process.cwd()` (which is why the parameter exists), `patch` is fetched from the wrong repository (or `gh` fails with "not a git repository"), while `baseSha`/`headSha`/`changedFiles` come from the intended repo — yielding a review of unrelated content or an immediate failure. Not verifiable further because no caller of runGithub exists in this checkout.

findings.title: Restore failing check conclusion when review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, postCheck() is called with conclusion "neutral" (was "failure"). A check run with conclusion neutral is treated as a non-blocking/passing result by GitHub required status checks, whereas "failure" blocks merge. So a review that errored (e.g. gh/git/model failure) now reports a passing gate and the PR can merge, even though the same check's summary text says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." The error signal that previously reached branch protection is downgraded to a value indistinguishable from the intended needs_human outcome (VERDICT_CONCLUSION.needs_human = "neutral", src/adapters/github.ts:53).

This diff deletes that checkout and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR head (line 59) after `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51), with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 56) and job permissions `pull-requests: write` + `checks: write` (lines 18-19) on a self-hosted runner (line 23). findings.title: Restore severity normalization; lowercase severities now downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code normalized the raw value first: `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase();` then tested `SEVERITIES.includes(sev)`. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` directly, so any value that is not already an exact uppercase enum member now fails the guard and falls through to the default. Substitution: severity="p0" -> SEVERITIES.includes("p0") @src/shared/schema.ts:97 rejects -> severity becomes "P3" @src/shared/schema.ts:99 (a critical finding silently reported as lowest priority); severity="P1 " (trailing whitespace, previously trimmed) -> rejects -> "P3"; severity=undefined -> rejects -> "P3". The same hunk also changes the fallback from the conservative "P1" to "P3", so malformed/absent severities are now buried as low-risk rather than surfaced. normalizeReview maps every model-produced finding through this function (@src/shared/schema.ts:132), and downstream verdict/ordering consumes severity, so a P0/P1 can be demoted to P3.

findings.title: normalizeFinding drops case/whitespace normalization, silently downgrading severity
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the untrusted-input normalization layer: normalizeReview (line 132) maps it over `raw.findings` parsed from arbitrary LLM JSON as `any`, so runtime values are not constrained to uppercase Severity. Base code computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and validated that, so "p1", " P0 ", "p2\n" all normalized to valid severities. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` directly, so any value that is not already exactly "P0".."P3" fails the guard and is replaced by the fallback. Compounded by the default changing from "P1" to "P3", a valid high-severity finding emitted lowercase ("p0"/"p1") is now silently downgraded to P3, and a missing severity becomes P3 instead of P1. This makes a parse failure indistinguishable from a real P3 and can let a critical finding slip past the review gate.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; lowercase severities silently become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, normalizeFinding computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and used `sev` for the SEVERITIES membership check, falling back to "P1". The new body passes the raw, un-normalized value straight into `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` and falls back to "P3". Substituting a common LLM output value: `raw.severity = "p0"` -> `SEVERITIES.includes("p0")` is false -> branch taken = fallback -> result "P3". Same for `" p0"`, `"P0 "`, `"p1"`, etc. A genuine P0/P1 is therefore silently reclassified to the lowest severity (previously "p0" normalized to "P0", and any other invalid value fell back to the more conservative "P1"). Because severity is the sole signal a caller uses to rank/act on findings, this both hides critical findings and removes the ability to distinguish a parse failure from a legitimately-P3 finding. This is an exported/public normalizer for untrusted model JSON (Partial<Finding> is a compile-time lie about runtime input), so the swallow site is the contract defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Restore token stripping before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes both the `const env = { ...process.env }` copy with `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` and the `env,` option passed to spawnSync. With no `env` option, spawnSync defaults to inheriting `process.env`, so the `codex exec` child now receives the three GitHub credentials the previous code deliberately stripped. codex exec is a model-driven process that runs against repo content and can read its own environment (and print/forward it), so this is a credential-exposure regression on the very path the deleted code guarded.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR deletes the explicit `env` sanitization (`delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN`) and the `env` option passed to spawnSync. Node's spawnSync defaults `env` to the full `process.env`, so the `codex exec` child (and any command/code it runs, e.g. via prompt-injected repo contents) now receives live GitHub credentials it was previously denied. The read-only sandbox does not remove env vars or block network, so a review run against an untrusted PR can exfiltrate or misuse the token — a supply-chain/credential-exposure regression on the exact path this agent runs in CI.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The hunk deletes the `const env = { ...process.env }` copy plus `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN`, and removes the `env` option from the `spawnSync` call at line 23. With no `env` option, Node's spawnSync inherits the full parent `process.env` (documented default), so the external `codex` binary — and any tool it in turn launches — now receives the reviewer's GitHub credentials. The `-s read-only` flag only sandboxes filesystem writes; it does not restrict environment access or network egress, so the tokens are reachable/exfiltratable by the subprocess. The previous code deliberately deleted all three token names, so this is a clear regression, not a no-op cleanup.

findings.title: Restore fork guard so untrusted PRs cannot run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control preventing fork-originated PRs from running this job. Without it the `pull_request` job runs on a self-hosted runner for any fork PR, then checks out attacker-controlled code (actions/checkout@v4 with ref=head.sha, line 23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, executes package lifecycle scripts from the fork) and executes the fork's own `src/cli.ts` (line 34). That is arbitrary code execution on persistent self-hosted infrastructure, and the job exposes `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (lines 33-34) plus `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` permissions (lines 13-14). Fork PRs get a read-only token and no repo secrets, so this is primarily runner/infrastructure compromise rather than direct secret exfiltration, but it is still an untrusted-code execution path the guard existed to block.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted fork PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate restricting this `pull_request` workflow to same-repo branches. With it gone, the job runs for fork PRs, and the workflow checks out the attacker-controlled head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, fetch-depth 0), then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (executes the fork's lifecycle/postinstall scripts) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` on a `self-hosted` runner. That is arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host by any external contributor, before any token/secret limitation applies — the attacker can exfiltrate runner credentials, poison the runner for subsequent trusted runs, or pivot to the host network. GitHub explicitly warns against self-hosted runners on public repos for exactly this reason.

findings.title: Fork PRs now run untrusted code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deletes `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` (base line 19), the only guard restricting the job to PRs from this repository. With it gone, the `pull_request`-triggered job runs for fork PRs on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner, checks out the fork's head via `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (line 23), and executes fork-controlled code: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs the fork's lifecycle/postinstall scripts, then `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts ...` (line 34) runs the fork's source. That is arbitrary code execution on persistent, trusted infrastructure reachable by any external contributor, enabling exfiltration of other jobs' data, cached credentials, and network/metadata endpoints on the runner. The removed guard was the sole mitigation; there is no `pull_request_target`/environment protection elsewhere in the repo (only this workflow exists).

findings.title: 0 duration now silently ignored, overriding explicit env config
findings.whyItBreaks: Precondition substitution: value="0" -> trimmed="0" (line 132, not empty) -> Number("0")=0 -> `Number.isFinite(0) && 0 > 0` is false @line 135 -> returns fallbackMs instead of 0. Before this diff the same input returned 0. The base code explicitly accepted 0 (`parsed >= 0`), so 0 was a valid, user-settable duration. findings.title: formatDuration can render invalid 'Xm 60s'/'60s' output
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is computed as Math.floor(ms/60000) while seconds is rounded independently via Math.round((ms%60000)/1000). When the sub-minute remainder is >= 59500ms the remainder rounds up to 60, so the function returns e.g. ms=119999 -> '1m 60s' (and ms=59999 -> '60s' instead of '1m 0s'). The previous code rounded total seconds first, so the remainder could never be 60. These strings are emitted verbatim into the review markdown at lines 75 and 80, so users see an impossible duration.

The new code rounds minutes and seconds from separate quantities, so the seconds term can round up to 60 without carrying into minutes. Concrete values: ms=59999 → minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → "60s" (base rendered "1m 0s"); ms=119999 → minutes=1, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → "1m 60s" (base rendered "2m 0s"). These render into the PR-review markdown stats line (formatDuration call sites src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: Normalize formatDuration so seconds never reaches 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes and seconds independently: minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms%60000)/1000). Rounding the remainder on its own lets seconds equal 60 instead of carrying into minutes. For ms=119999: minutes=floor(119999/60000)=1 and seconds=round(59999/1000)=60, yielding the malformed string "1m 60s" (the pre-change code returned "2m 0s"). For ms=59500..59999 it yields "60s". This is rendered into the stats line of every review output (render.ts:75 and render.ts:80), so the regression is user-visible.
